nodes.rationale: The original lab enabled DNS on two servers with a conflicting malformed record; split-brain DNS is a real production defect, so only Server1 now answers.

nodes.label: Notes versus lab disagreements
nodes.rationale: The original notes claimed a working demo but three claims did not work in the lab: sales@gmail.com, DNS on two servers with a leading-space record, and the mail chain around the domain.

nodes.label: Why keep the original notes
nodes.rationale: Honesty (show how the work was really done), reproducibility (apply_fixes.py regenerates the hardened lab from the pristine .pkt) and reference (the Bengali PDF is the most concise PAT/ISP description).

nodes.label: Email Server not found root cause
nodes.norm_label: email server not found root cause
nodes.rationale: The mail server Domain Name field was blank. SMTP, POP3 and the users were correct, but with no domain configured the server rejected every connection.

nodes.norm_label: the .pkt file is an encrypted container
nodes.rationale: A proprietary encrypted .pkt cannot be diffed or reviewed in a pull request, so the repository extracts the plaintext XML and generates everything else from it.

nodes.label: Why there are two .pkt files
nodes.rationale: Keeping the pristine original makes the audit reproducible and documents the honest starting point instead of pretending the project was built this way from the start.

nodes.label: pkt-core dependency
nodes.rationale: pkt-core decrypts the proprietary Cisco Packet Tracer .pkt container so the lab can be diffed, audited and exported as plain text.

nodes.label: pkt-core version pin note

nodes.label: C-04 DHCP pool could lease SVI/HSRP addresses
nodes.norm_label: c-04 dhcp pool could lease svi/hsrp addresses
nodes.rationale: Only .1-.20 and .254 were excluded, leaving the .252/.253 core SVIs allocatable and causing intermittent black-holed clients; .252-.253 are now excluded on all seven pools with explicit ranges.

nodes.label: H-03 core-02 had no DHCP relay path
nodes.norm_label: h-03 core-02 had no dhcp relay path
nodes.rationale: If HSRP made core-02 active for a VLAN no client could obtain a lease; ip helper-address 10.1.1.1 was added to its user SVIs.

nodes.label: Centralized DHCP - core-01 for seven networks
nodes.norm_label: centralized dhcp - core-01 for seven networks

nodes.label: Why DHCP relay instead of a DHCP server per branch
nodes.norm_label: why dhcp relay instead of a dhcp server per branch
nodes.rationale: Centralisation is the point of the project and the DNS address is then defined once and cannot drift between sites; the trade-off is a single point of failure at core-01, mitigated by the relay on core-02.

nodes.label: Why a single DHCP server in the HQ core
nodes.norm_label: why a single dhcp server in the hq core
nodes.rationale: DHCP is inherently chatty and centralised management is the point of the project. core-01 is the only DHCP server and core-02 relays via ip helper-address, so the active HSRP gateway always has a working DHCP path and the DNS address reaches every client automatically.

nodes.label: Running-configs exported directly from lab/main_project.pkt
nodes.rationale: Configurations are exported rather than typed by hand so documentation and the lab cannot drift apart.

nodes.label: DHCP to DNS integration
nodes.rationale: The dns-server 172.10.10.2 line in every pool is the heart of the project: every client learns the central DNS address together with its IP and gateway, with no manual configuration.

nodes.label: DHCP client DNS field greyed out
nodes.norm_label: dhcp client dns field greyed out
nodes.rationale: A PC configured as a DHCP client cannot edit its DNS field; it is controlled by the DHCP scope. This is the single most common confusion in the project.

nodes.label: Single DHCP server trade-off
nodes.rationale: New leases stop if core-01 fails; core-02 has a helper address but the pools only exist on core-01, so production would use DHCP failover or a dedicated server.

nodes.label: Server services configuration and DNS A records
nodes.norm_label: server services configuration and dns a records

nodes.label: Single authoritative DNS rule
nodes.rationale: Only one server may run DNS: two servers with different zone data is split-brain DNS and produces unpredictable results.

nodes.label: Why a dedicated server VLAN
nodes.rationale: Isolation and segmentation: the servers are the most critical asset, so they get their own broadcast domain, subnet and gateway; a broadcast storm on a user VLAN can never reach them and ACLs can treat server traffic differently.

nodes.label: Topology poster (1920x1080 rendered diagram)
nodes.rationale: Visual poster: four branch sites feed HQ (access, leaf, core and server VLAN 20), then EDGE-RTR, ISP and Server3; it advertises 42 devices, 6 sites, 8 VLANs and 4 IPsec tunnels and includes a PAT proof panel.

nodes.label: Internet edge addressing (200.1.1.1/30)
nodes.rationale: 200.1.1.1 is the single address every internal host is translated to on the way out, the proof point for the PAT demonstration.

nodes.label: Why /30 on the ISP link
nodes.rationale: A point-to-point link needs exactly two usable addresses; /30 provides exactly that, while /24 would waste 252 addresses and advertise a network that does not exist.

nodes.label: RFC 5737 TEST-NET-3 for the simulated Internet
nodes.norm_label: rfc 5737 test-net-3 for the simulated internet
nodes.rationale: 203.0.113.0/24 is a documentation range so the simulated Internet can never collide with a real network.

nodes.label: Encrypted WAN (IPsec AES plus SHA-HMAC)
nodes.rationale: Only the intended traffic is tunnelled using interesting-traffic ACLs mirrored at both ends of every HQ to branch link.

nodes.label: IPsec tunnel down states (QM, dormant, active)
nodes.norm_label: ipsec tunnel down states (qm, dormant, active)

nodes.label: IKE Diffie-Hellman group 2 (legacy)
nodes.rationale: Kept at group 2 because the 2811 image in Packet Tracer 9 implements a limited set of IKE groups and groups 14 and higher produced SA rekey failures in testing; production should use group 14.

nodes.label: Pre-shared key VPN123 (weak)
nodes.rationale: The key must be identical on five devices; changing it means editing five configs and re-testing four tunnels before every demonstration. The project demonstrates the mechanism of IPsec, not key distribution.

nodes.label: Access port security (portfast, bpduguard, sticky MAC)
nodes.norm_label: access port security (portfast, bpduguard, sticky mac)

nodes.label: Access-layer hardening (portfast, bpduguard, port-security)
nodes.rationale: portfast removes the 30-second STP convergence delay; bpduguard shuts a port if a switch is connected, preventing a rogue-switch loop; port-security pins one MAC per port to stop flooding and spoofing.

nodes.label: Port down after device replacement (sticky MAC)
nodes.norm_label: port down after device replacement (sticky mac)

nodes.label: 192.186.x.x label typo
nodes.rationale: Branch PCs were originally labelled 192.186, a typo for 192.168 that is not even a private range; they always used DHCP from the correct pools, so only the label was wrong.

nodes.label: T-20 branch Internet reachability
nodes.rationale: The strongest single test: the branch has no ISP link at all, yet the traffic travels over the IPsec WAN to HQ, is translated by EDGE-RTR, and reaches the Internet server.

nodes.label: Why /24 everywhere
nodes.rationale: One subnet per department is the right granularity for a small network; the only exception is the ISP link at /30, which gives exactly two usable addresses.

nodes.label: Configuration build order
nodes.rationale: Each step depends on the previous one: naming and cabling, VLANs, core SVIs and HSRP, DHCP pools, OSPF, IPsec, branch SVIs and relay, NAT/PAT, server services, then clients.

nodes.label: HSRP first-hop gateway redundancy
nodes.rationale: core-01 is active (priority 110 plus preempt) and core-02 standby; the shared .254 virtual gateway lets clients keep working if the active core fails.

nodes.label: NAT/PAT at the Internet edge
nodes.rationale: The overload keyword turns NAT into PAT: many inside sessions share one outside address, distinguished by the TCP/UDP source port.

nodes.label: OSPF area 0 across all six sites
nodes.norm_label: ospf area 0 across all six sites
nodes.rationale: default-information originate is what makes the branches Internet-capable without a direct ISP connection.

nodes.label: Branch default route via OSPF
nodes.rationale: The branch learns the Internet path through OSPF, so it does not require a direct ISP connection; traffic is sent toward HQ first.

nodes.label: PAT (Port Address Translation)
nodes.rationale: PAT lets many internal hosts share one external address 200.1.1.1 by giving each session a distinct source port.

nodes.label: PAT ACL (access-list 1)
nodes.rationale: The standard ACL is used for NAT matching, not as a security control; the security controls are the named extended ACLs on the core.

nodes.label: Department isolation ACLs
nodes.rationale: The ACLs live on core-01 only because it is always the active gateway; a production build applies the same ACL on both cores so a failover cannot leave a VLAN unfiltered.

nodes.label: Branch cannot reach the Internet
nodes.rationale: The most common cause by far is default-information originate missing on core-01; without it OSPF never advertises the default route and every branch is an island.

nodes.label: Branch-to-branch traffic fails by design
nodes.rationale: Only Sales to branch pairs are tunnelled; there is no interesting-traffic ACL and no crypto map for a branch-to-branch pair.

nodes.label: bootpc/bootps DHCP permit rule
nodes.rationale: The permit udp any eq bootpc any eq bootps line is first so DHCP renewals of neighbouring departments still work; without it a client gets an IP but loses the DNS server.

nodes.label: Static routes at the edge
nodes.rationale: An edge router should have the simplest control plane; two summary routes are easier to audit than an OSPF adjacency and remove any chance of a routing loop between the OSPF domain and the translation device.

nodes.label: Random connectivity loss (pool overlaps SVI)
nodes.rationale: The original exclusions covered only .1-.20 and .254, leaving .252 and .253 (the two core SVI addresses) inside the allocatable range; the fix is to exclude .252-.254.

nodes.label: Lessons learned: consistency and automation
nodes.rationale: The hard part is consistency between configuration commands: a wrong mail domain, an overlapping DHCP pool, two disagreeing DNS servers and duplicate hostnames are invisible in a topology screenshot, which is why the audit was automated.

nodes.label: Why OSPF over RIP
nodes.rationale: OSPF is link-state with a full topology view, fast convergence and authentication; RIP 30-second hold-down and 15-hop limit do not scale, and OSPF also originates the default route.

nodes.label: No inbound NAT mapping
nodes.rationale: The PAT ACL matches only inside networks and only 200.1.1.1 is visible on a /30, so an external host cannot initiate a session to internal servers.

nodes.label: Generate traffic before showing the PAT proof
nodes.norm_label: generate traffic before showing the pat proof
nodes.rationale: Dynamic PAT entries expire after a period of inactivity, so real ping traffic must be generated first or the translation table can look empty.

nodes.norm_label: dns could not find host diagnosis

nodes.norm_label: symptom to diagnose to fix pattern
nodes.rationale: Work from the bottom up and never change two things at once.

nodes.norm_label: c-01 sales mail client used the wrong domain
nodes.rationale: The server only accepts mail for its own company.com domain, so sales@gmail.com broke the centrepiece Sales-to-HR email demo; MAIL_ID was corrected and the stored test message rewritten.

nodes.label: H-04 Web server served the Packet Tracer default page
nodes.norm_label: h-04 web server served the packet tracer default page
nodes.rationale: A stock Cisco splash page is not a credible company web server, so it was replaced by a corporate intranet portal that makes the browser window evidence during the demo.

nodes.label: Corporate portal replaces the default splash page
nodes.norm_label: corporate portal replaces the default splash page
nodes.rationale: The page lists the service catalogue, DNS names, IP plan and gateways so the browser window itself becomes evidence during the demonstration.

nodes.label: Mail client must use the hostname, not the IP address
nodes.norm_label: mail client must use the hostname, not the ip address
nodes.rationale: Using mail.company.com forces resolution through the centralised DNS server, which proves DNS and mail working together.

nodes.label: Exactly one server may run the DNS service
nodes.norm_label: exactly one server may run the dns service
nodes.rationale: Two DNS servers with different zone data are split-brain DNS and produce non-deterministic client results.

nodes.label: The SMTP domain field must be set
nodes.norm_label: the smtp domain field must be set
nodes.rationale: With SMTP and POP3 enabled but the domain blank the server rejects every session and the client reports Server not found even though DNS and IP connectivity are perfect - a real defect in the original build.

nodes.label: Access layer - dual-homed switches and port hardening
nodes.norm_label: access layer - dual-homed switches and port hardening
nodes.rationale: Each access switch trunks to both leaf switches so a single leaf failure never isolates a department; every host port is hardened with portfast, bpduguard and sticky-MAC port-security.

nodes.label: Three-tier campus with routed WAN and PAT edge
nodes.norm_label: three-tier campus with routed wan and pat edge

nodes.label: Leaf/Core layer - spine-and-leaf, HSRP and SVIs
nodes.norm_label: leaf/core layer - spine-and-leaf, hsrp and svis

nodes.label: PortFast and BPDU guard on access ports
nodes.norm_label: portfast and bpdu guard on access ports
nodes.rationale: portfast removes the 30-second STP convergence delay from an edge port, bpduguard shuts the port if a switch is plugged into it, and port-security with a sticky MAC pins exactly one host per port.

nodes.label: Security architecture - ACLs, IPsec, HSRP, port-security
nodes.norm_label: security architecture - acls, ipsec, hsrp, port-security

nodes.label: WAN/Distribution layer - HQ-WAN-RTR hub with four IPsec tunnels
nodes.norm_label: wan/distribution layer - hq-wan-rtr hub with four ipsec tunnels

nodes.label: H-06 No portfast or BPDU guard on access ports
nodes.norm_label: h-06 no portfast or bpdu guard on access ports

nodes.label: Accepted trade-off - Layer-2 loop between the leaves
nodes.norm_label: accepted trade-off - layer-2 loop between the leaves
nodes.rationale: Both leaves trunk to both access switches and to each other, creating an L2 loop that PVST blocks; in production the leaf-to-leaf link would be removed or access switches single-homed, but it is accepted for the teaching topology.

nodes.label: Why LACP between the two leaf switches
nodes.norm_label: why lacp between the two leaf switches
nodes.rationale: The leaf pair already has two independent paths to two independent cores; the port-channel aggregates bandwidth for east-west traffic and gives L2 redundancy when a single link fails.

nodes.label: Why static routes on EDGE-RTR
nodes.rationale: An edge router should have the simplest possible control plane; two summary routes are easier to audit than an OSPF adjacency and remove the possibility of a loop between the OSPF domain and the NAT device.

nodes.label: pkt-core open-source Packet Tracer reverse-engineering library
nodes.norm_label: pkt-core open-source packet tracer reverse-engineering library

nodes.label: Why a single OSPF area
nodes.rationale: The WAN is a five-node star, so a flat area keeps one OSPF database, fast convergence and no area-boundary summarisation to explain; area design would only be worthwhile beyond roughly 30 routers.

nodes.label: Why branch traffic is encrypted
nodes.rationale: Each branch link carries site-to-site IPsec with a matching crypto map and ACL pair on both ends so only the intended source/destination pairs are tunnelled.

nodes.label: Why HSRP on the user VLANs
nodes.norm_label: why hsrp on the user vlans
nodes.rationale: core-01 holds priority 110 and core-02 the default 100; both carry the same SVIs so a core failure is transparent to the client.
